def: Small obligate intracellular gram-negative bacteria spread by arthropod vectors (ticks, lice, fleas, mites). They cause Rocky Mountain spotted fever, typhus and related rickettsial diseases, typically with fever and a rash.

Obligate intracellular bacterium with an elementary body/reticulate body life cycle. Causes the most common bacterial STI (urethritis, cervicitis, PID), lymphogranuloma venereum, and trachoma, a leading infectious cause of blindness.

Drugs that block muscarinic acetylcholine receptors, reducing parasympathetic effects. Examples are atropine, ipratropium and oxybutynin; effects include dry mouth, pupil dilation, urinary retention and tachycardia.

Enzymes that transfer a phosphate from ATP onto tyrosine residues of proteins, switching signaling pathways on. Mutated or overactive forms drive cancers (BCR-ABL in CML, EGFR, HER2) and are blocked by drugs such as imatinib.
Darkening of an area of skin from excess melanin. Seen in melasma, post-inflammatory change, Addison disease (from raised ACTH/MSH) and acanthosis nigricans.
A benign tumor of the anterior pituitary, often secreting one hormone (prolactin most commonly). Large tumors can compress the optic chiasm, causing bitemporal hemianopia.

The neurotransmitter of motor neurons at the neuromuscular junction, autonomic ganglia and parasympathetic targets. Acts on nicotinic and muscarinic receptors and is broken down by acetylcholinesterase.

Deliberate or disease-related dampening of immune activity, such as with glucocorticoids, calcineurin inhibitors or antimetabolites to prevent transplant rejection. Raises the risk of opportunistic infection and certain cancers.

An antiepileptic that blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, used for tonic-clonic and partial seizures. Notable toxicities are gingival hyperplasia, hirsutism, nystagmus, megaloblastic anemia and teratogenicity (fetal hydantoin syndrome).

Life-threatening low blood pressure from systemic infection that persists despite fluids, caused by widespread vasodilation and capillary leak. Often triggered by gram-negative endotoxin (lipopolysaccharide).

A highly contagious paramyxovirus infection with fever, cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots in the mouth and a descending maculopapular rash. Complications include pneumonia, encephalitis and SSPE.

Descending upper motor neuron pathways from motor cortex. Corticospinal fibers decussate at the medullary pyramids to control contralateral limb movement; corticobulbar fibers supply cranial nerve motor nuclei.
A small single-stranded DNA virus family. Human parvovirus B19 causes erythema infectiosum (fifth disease) and aplastic crises in people with chronic hemolytic anemia.

Inflammation of the peritoneum, usually from bacterial infection. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis occurs in cirrhosis with ascites; secondary peritonitis follows bowel perforation. Presents with abdominal pain and rigidity.

An enduring, inflexible pattern of inner experience and behavior that deviates from cultural norms and causes impairment, beginning in adolescence or early adulthood. Grouped into clusters A (odd), B (dramatic) and C (anxious).
Encapsulated, alpha-hemolytic, optochin-sensitive gram-positive diplococcus. The leading cause of community-acquired pneumonia, otitis media and adult meningitis; also causes sinusitis.

Implantation of a fertilized egg outside the uterine cavity, most often in the fallopian tube. Presents with pain and bleeding, and rupture is a surgical emergency. Risk is raised by prior PID or tubal surgery.

Bacteriostatic antibiotics that bind the 30S ribosomal subunit and block tRNA attachment (doxycycline, minocycline). Cover rickettsiae, chlamydia and Lyme disease; they discolor developing teeth and are avoided in pregnancy and children.
Acute spreading infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, causing warm, red, tender skin. Usually due to Streptococcus pyogenes or Staphylococcus aureus.

Cancer of the uterine lining, typically presenting as postmenopausal bleeding. Linked to unopposed estrogen (obesity, anovulation, tamoxifen); type I is estrogen-driven endometrioid, with PTEN mutations common.
Signaling molecules derived from tyrosine that contain a catechol ring: dopamine, norepinephrine and epinephrine. They act as neurotransmitters and adrenal hormones on adrenergic receptors.

The paired branch of the abdominal aorta that supplies each kidney. Narrowing (atherosclerosis or fibromuscular dysplasia) causes renovascular hypertension through activation of the renin-angiotensin system.
The inner mucosal lining of the uterus that thickens under estrogen and progesterone, then sheds during menstruation. It is where the embryo implants.
A tough fibrous structural protein forming intermediate filaments in epithelial cells, hair and nails. Cytokeratin staining is used to identify carcinomas.
The final segment of the small intestine, which absorbs vitamin B12 and bile salts. Disease or resection (as in Crohn disease) causes B12 deficiency and bile acid malabsorption.
Cranial nerve I, carrying smell from olfactory epithelium through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone to the olfactory bulb. Fractures of the cribriform plate can cause anosmia.

Inherited thickening of the left ventricular wall, often asymmetric septal, from sarcomere gene mutations (beta-myosin heavy chain). Can obstruct outflow and cause sudden cardiac death in young athletes.

Repeated pauses in breathing during sleep, most commonly from upper airway collapse (obstructive) in obese patients. Causes daytime sleepiness and snoring, and raises risk of hypertension and arrhythmia.

Infection of the middle ear space behind the tympanic membrane, common in children. Usually follows viral upper respiratory infection; causative bacteria are S. pneumoniae, nontypeable H. influenzae and Moraxella catarrhalis.

A small gram-negative coccobacillus requiring factors X and V to grow. Encapsulated type b causes meningitis and epiglottitis in unvaccinated children; nontypeable strains cause otitis media and COPD exacerbations.
Water inside cells, about two-thirds of total body water. Rich in potassium and phosphate, in contrast to extracellular fluid, which is rich in sodium and chloride.
A surgical incision through the abdominal wall to open the abdominal cavity, used for exploration or to treat intra-abdominal disease.

The terminal segment of the GI tract. Above the pectinate line it has visceral innervation and drains to internal iliac nodes; below it has somatic innervation and drains to superficial inguinal nodes. The external anal sphincter is skeletal muscle.
Enzyme that synthesizes new DNA by adding nucleotides to a primer in the 5' to 3' direction. Prokaryotic DNA pol III replicates and also proofreads; pol I removes RNA primers.
Abnormal involuntary movements. Includes tardive dyskinesia from long-term antipsychotics and levodopa-induced chorea in Parkinson disease; hemiballismus and asterixis are specific forms.
The first product of the TCA cycle, formed from acetyl-CoA and oxaloacetate. Also acts as a calcium chelator in anticoagulated stored blood and an allosteric activator of fatty acid synthesis.

Stretch-sensitive nerve endings in the carotid sinus and aortic arch that sense blood pressure and signal the brainstem via cranial nerves IX and X. Falling pressure triggers increased sympathetic outflow.
A class of plasma proteins that includes immunoglobulins and transport proteins. Gamma globulins are antibodies; a monoclonal spike suggests multiple myeloma.

Infection by Candida yeasts. Causes oral thrush, vaginitis and esophagitis in immunosuppressed patients, and invasive bloodstream disease in the critically ill. Treated with azole or echinocandin antifungals.
Loss of the myelin sheath around axons, slowing or blocking nerve conduction. Seen in multiple sclerosis, Guillain-Barre syndrome, and progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy.
Double-membrane organelles that make most cellular ATP by oxidative phosphorylation and house the TCA cycle. They have their own maternally inherited DNA.
One of the alternative versions of a gene at a given locus. A person inherits one allele from each parent.

Elevated blood ketone bodies (acetoacetate, beta-hydroxybutyrate) made by the liver from fatty acids during fasting, starvation or insulin deficiency. When severe it causes acidosis, as in diabetic ketoacidosis.

Impaired conduction from atria to ventricles. First degree is a prolonged PR interval, second degree has dropped beats (Mobitz I or II), and third degree is complete dissociation of atria and ventricles.
A fat-soluble vitamin needed to carboxylate clotting factors II, VII, IX, X and proteins C and S. Deficiency or warfarin causes bleeding; newborns receive an injection to prevent hemorrhagic disease.
Small airways without cartilage that lead from bronchi to alveoli. They are lined by club cells, and respiratory bronchioles are the first to have alveoli in their walls.
A fluid-filled skin blister larger than 1 cm (smaller ones are vesicles), seen in pemphigus, bullous pemphigoid and burns. Also an air-filled space in emphysematous lung.
Spastic paralysis from tetanospasmin, a toxin of Clostridium tetani that blocks release of GABA and glycine from inhibitory neurons. Causes lockjaw (trismus), muscle spasms and opisthotonos.

Sexually transmitted infection by Neisseria gonorrhoeae, a gram-negative diplococcus. Causes urethritis, cervicitis, PID and can disseminate to cause septic arthritis; newborns can acquire conjunctivitis.

Infection by the protozoan Toxoplasma gondii, from cat feces or undercooked meat. Causes ring-enhancing brain lesions in AIDS and congenital infection with hydrocephalus, chorioretinitis and intracranial calcifications.
Drugs that block acetylcholine receptors, typically muscarinic ones. Cause dry mouth, mydriasis, constipation, urinary retention and confusion in excess.

A cardiac glycoside that inhibits the Na+/K+ ATPase, raising intracellular calcium and increasing contractility; it also slows AV conduction. Toxicity causes nausea, yellow-tinted vision and arrhythmias, worsened by hypokalemia.
Enlargement of the thyroid gland. Causes include iodine deficiency, Graves disease and Hashimoto thyroiditis; it may be associated with hypo-, hyper- or normal thyroid function.
Formation of bone. Intramembranous ossification makes flat skull bones directly from mesenchyme; endochondral ossification replaces a cartilage model, as in long bones.
Hair loss. Androgenetic alopecia is the common patterned form driven by dihydrotestosterone; alopecia areata is autoimmune and patchy.
Excess aldosterone causing hypertension, hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis with low renin. Primary form (Conn syndrome) is from an adrenal adenoma or hyperplasia.
The brainstem region between the midbrain and medulla, containing motor nuclei of CN V through VIII, the pontine respiratory centers, and fibers linking the cerebrum and cerebellum.

Paired embryonic structures that form the head and neck, each with its own artery, nerve, cartilage and muscle. Clefts are the external grooves between arches; failed closure gives branchial cleft cysts.
An enzyme that removes a phosphate group from a substrate by hydrolysis. Opposes kinases; alkaline phosphatase is a marker of cholestasis and bone turnover.
Development of secondary sexual characteristics before age 8 in girls or 9 in boys. Central form comes from early GnRH axis activation; peripheral forms arise from sex steroids made elsewhere.

Drugs that block the Na+/Cl- cotransporter in the distal convoluted tubule (hydrochlorothiazide, chlorthalidone). Used for hypertension; cause hypokalemia, hyponatremia, hypercalcemia and hyperglycemia, and reduce urinary calcium.

The largest lipoproteins, assembled in intestinal cells to carry dietary triglycerides through the lymph to the blood. Their ApoB-48 is required for assembly; lipoprotein lipase removes their triglycerides.
Particles of lipid wrapped in phospholipid and apolipoprotein that transport fats in blood: chylomicrons, VLDL, IDL, LDL and HDL.

Raised pressure within the skull, causing headache, vomiting, papilledema and, if severe, Cushing triad (hypertension, bradycardia, irregular breathing). Idiopathic intracranial hypertension typically affects obese young women.

Recurrent throbbing, usually unilateral headache with nausea and sensitivity to light and sound, sometimes preceded by aura. Thought to involve trigeminovascular activation and CGRP; treated with triptans.

Primary adrenal insufficiency, most often from autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex. Causes low cortisol and aldosterone with fatigue, hypotension, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia and skin hyperpigmentation.
The volume of blood ejected by the left ventricle per beat, equal to end-diastolic minus end-systolic volume. Cardiac output equals stroke volume times heart rate.
Bone-forming cells that secrete osteoid and promote mineralization. Their activity is reflected by serum alkaline phosphatase, and they release RANKL to activate osteoclasts.
The cytosolic pathway that converts glucose to pyruvate, yielding 2 net ATP and 2 NADH. Phosphofructokinase-1 is the rate-limiting step.

Cranial nerve VII, supplying muscles of facial expression, taste to the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, and lacrimal and salivary glands. Exits the skull via the stylomastoid foramen; injury causes Bell palsy.
Misfolded protein that aggregates as insoluble beta-pleated sheet fibrils in tissues. Stains with Congo red and shows apple-green birefringence under polarized light.
Hormones or drugs that act at the progesterone receptor, such as medroxyprogesterone and levonorgestrel. Used in contraception and to oppose estrogen's effect on the endometrium.
The number of CD4+ helper T cells per microliter of blood, used to monitor HIV. Counts below 200 define AIDS and trigger prophylaxis against opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis.
The addition of a phosphate group to a molecule, usually by a kinase using ATP. A major way to switch enzyme and signaling protein activity on or off.

A tear in the aortic intima that lets blood split the wall layers, causing sudden tearing chest or back pain. Risk factors are hypertension and connective tissue disease; type A involves the ascending aorta.
Antidepressants that block reuptake of both serotonin and norepinephrine, such as venlafaxine and duloxetine. Also used for neuropathic pain and anxiety; can raise blood pressure.
The major artery of the neck. The common carotid divides into the external carotid (face and neck) and internal carotid (brain and eye). Atherosclerosis at the bifurcation is a cause of stroke.
Inflammation of artery walls, as in giant cell (temporal) arteritis and Takayasu arteritis. Can narrow vessels and cause ischemia.

An autoimmune reaction following group A streptococcal pharyngitis that causes carditis, migratory arthritis, chorea, erythema marginatum and subcutaneous nodules. Molecular mimicry damages the heart valves, especially the mitral valve.
Clumping of platelets at a vessel injury to form the primary hemostatic plug, mediated by fibrinogen bridging glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptors. Inhibited by aspirin, clopidogrel and abciximab.

Superficial fungal skin infection by dermatophytes, causing scaly, ring-shaped itchy lesions. Named by site: tinea corporis (body, ringworm), capitis, pedis, cruris and unguium. Diagnosed by KOH prep showing hyphae.
An extra whooshing sound heard during the cardiac cycle from turbulent blood flow, usually caused by valve disease or shunts. Classified as systolic or diastolic by timing.
Bacteria with no cell wall, so they are not seen on Gram stain and are resistant to beta-lactams. Mycoplasma pneumoniae causes atypical (walking) pneumonia with cold agglutinins.
A gas made from arginine by nitric oxide synthase that relaxes vascular smooth muscle via cGMP, causing vasodilation. It mediates the effects of nitrates and PDE-5 inhibitors.
The connective tissue layer of skin beneath the epidermis, containing collagen, blood vessels, nerves, glands and hair follicles.
Drugs that relax vascular smooth muscle and lower blood pressure, such as hydralazine, nitrates and calcium channel blockers. Can cause reflex tachycardia and headache.
A fat-soluble vitamin (retinol) needed for vision, epithelial differentiation and immunity. Deficiency causes night blindness and xerophthalmia; excess is teratogenic and causes hepatotoxicity.
Too little amniotic fluid, often from fetal renal malformation or rupture of membranes. Can cause Potter sequence with pulmonary hypoplasia and limb deformities.
A brain disorder with recurrent unprovoked seizures from abnormal synchronized neuronal firing. Seizures are focal or generalized; some focal seizures begin with an aura.
Inflammation of the heart muscle, most commonly from viral infection (coxsackie B). Presents with chest pain, heart failure or arrhythmia.

Disease from extracellular deposition of misfolded protein fibrils. AL type comes from light chains in plasma cell disorders; AA type follows chronic inflammation. Commonly affects kidney, heart and nerves.
Elevated blood urea nitrogen and creatinine from reduced glomerular filtration. Can be prerenal, intrinsic renal or postrenal in cause.
The ball of the hip joint, which fits into the acetabulum. Its blood supply from the medial circumflex femoral artery is vulnerable after femoral neck fracture, risking avascular necrosis.
Drugs that block acetylcholinesterase, raising acetylcholine at synapses. Used in myasthenia gravis (neostigmine, pyridostigmine) and Alzheimer disease (donepezil); excess causes cholinergic crisis.
A flagellated protozoan, Giardia lamblia, spread by cysts in contaminated water. Causes foul, fatty diarrhea and bloating; treated with metronidazole.
A cyclic amide. The beta-lactam ring is the core of penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems and monobactams, which inhibit cell wall synthesis.
The active, feeding and replicating form of a protozoan parasite, as opposed to the dormant cyst. Seen in Giardia, Entamoeba histolytica and malaria.
Long carbohydrate polymers made of many sugar units, such as starch, glycogen and cellulose. Bacterial capsule polysaccharides are poor antigens unless conjugated to protein.
Star-shaped glial cells of the CNS that support the blood-brain barrier, buffer extracellular potassium, take up neurotransmitters and form scar tissue. GFAP is their marker.

Drugs that block histamine receptors. H1 blockers treat allergy (first-generation like diphenhydramine are sedating; second-generation like loratadine are not); H2 blockers like famotidine reduce gastric acid.
A neutrophil enzyme that converts hydrogen peroxide into hypochlorous acid to kill microbes. Deficiency impairs killing, and it is the marker of myeloid cells like myeloblasts (Auer rods).
An autoimmune hyperthyroidism caused by antibodies that stimulate the TSH receptor. Features include diffuse goiter, exophthalmos and pretibial myxedema.
A two-carbon unit carried on coenzyme A, formed from pyruvate, fatty acids and ketogenic amino acids. It enters the TCA cycle and is the building block of cholesterol and fatty acids.
A class III antiarrhythmic that blocks potassium channels, prolonging the QT interval. Toxicities include pulmonary fibrosis, thyroid dysfunction, hepatotoxicity, corneal deposits and blue-gray skin.
Abnormal paleness of the skin and mucous membranes, as in anemia or poor perfusion.
A cytokine from macrophages and T cells that drives the acute-phase response (fever, CRP, hepcidin) and stimulates B cell differentiation. Blocked by tocilizumab in rheumatoid arthritis.
The enzyme (CYP19) that converts androgens to estrogens. It is found in ovarian granulosa cells and fat; inhibitors such as anastrozole treat breast cancer.
Effects of a cancer caused by hormones or immune responses rather than local tumor growth. Examples include SIADH and ACTH in small cell lung cancer and PTHrP in squamous cell carcinoma.
The vessel that carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. Pulmonary hypertension raises pressure here and loads the right heart.

A fetal vessel connecting the pulmonary artery to the aorta to bypass the lungs. It normally closes after birth; patent ductus gives a continuous machine-like murmur, kept open by prostaglandin E and closed by indomethacin.

A mold with septate hyphae branching at acute angles. Causes allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis, aspergilloma in old cavities, and invasive disease in neutropenia; some species produce aflatoxin.

X-linked enzyme defect that reduces NADPH, leaving red cells vulnerable to oxidative stress and hemolysis. Triggered by infection, fava beans and drugs like primaquine; Heinz bodies and bite cells are seen.
Cancer of myeloid precursors in bone marrow. Acute myeloid leukemia shows myeloblasts with Auer rods; chronic myeloid leukemia is driven by the Philadelphia chromosome and BCR-ABL.
Whooping cough, caused by Bordetella pertussis. Marked by severe paroxysmal cough ending in an inspiratory whoop, with lymphocytosis; pertussis toxin raises cAMP by inhibiting Gi.
CD4+ lymphocytes that coordinate immune responses by secreting cytokines, activating B cells, macrophages and cytotoxic T cells. Th1 and Th2 are major subsets; HIV destroys them.

Combination treatment for HIV using three or more drugs, typically two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors plus an integrase inhibitor, protease inhibitor or NNRTI. Suppresses viral load and restores CD4 counts.

Aerobic gram-negative rod producing blue-green pigment (pyocyanin) with a grape-like odor. Causes infections in burns, cystic fibrosis, ventilated and neutropenic patients; ecthyma gangrenosum; hot tub folliculitis.
A break in the stomach or duodenal mucosa from acid and pepsin. Most are from Helicobacter pylori or NSAIDs; duodenal ulcers hurt before meals and gastric ulcers worsen with eating.
A muscarinic antagonist that dilates the pupil, speeds heart rate and dries secretions. Used for bradycardia and organophosphate poisoning; toxicity gives hot, dry, red, mad.
Cytokines that induce an antiviral state in cells. Types I (alpha and beta) block viral replication; interferon-gamma activates macrophages. Used to treat hepatitis B and C and multiple sclerosis.

Antiviral drugs that block the HIV protease, preventing cleavage of viral polyproteins into functional proteins (names end in -navir, such as ritonavir). Cause hyperglycemia, lipodystrophy and CYP450 inhibition.
Clouding of the eye lens that causes blurred vision and glare. Risk factors are age, diabetes, steroids, smoking and UV exposure.
Surgical removal of the uterus, sometimes with the cervix, ovaries and tubes, for fibroids, bleeding or cancer. The ureter lies near the uterine artery and is at risk of injury.
High blood pH from hyperventilation lowering CO2. Occurs with anxiety, pain, high altitude, pulmonary embolism and salicylate toxicity.
Protein toxins secreted by bacteria that cause specific disease effects, such as diphtheria, cholera and tetanus toxins. They are antigenic and can be converted into toxoid vaccines.
How readily fluid and proteins cross the capillary wall. Increased by histamine and inflammation, causing edema and hypotension.

Acute autoimmune demyelinating polyneuropathy causing ascending symmetric weakness and areflexia, often after Campylobacter or viral infection. CSF shows high protein with normal cell count; treated with IVIG or plasmapheresis.
A fluid-filled swelling arising from a joint capsule or tendon sheath, most often at the dorsal wrist. It is benign and filled with thick mucinous fluid.
Infection by Borrelia burgdorferi spread by Ixodes ticks. Causes erythema migrans, then facial palsy, meningitis, heart block and migratory arthritis; treated with doxycycline.
Twisting of a segment of intestine around its mesentery, causing obstruction and ischemia. Sigmoid and cecal are common in adults; midgut volvulus occurs with malrotation in infants.
The channels that carry bile from the liver to the duodenum. The common bile duct joins the pancreatic duct at the ampulla of Vater; blockage causes jaundice.
Billowing of the mitral leaflets into the left atrium in systole, causing a mid-systolic click and sometimes regurgitation. Associated with Marfan syndrome and myxomatous degeneration.
A heart sound heard between S1 and S2. Ejection murmurs (aortic stenosis) crescendo-decrescendo; holosystolic murmurs occur with mitral or tricuspid regurgitation and ventricular septal defect.
Encapsulated gram-negative diplococcus that causes meningitis and meningococcemia with petechial rash and Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome. Prophylaxis for contacts is rifampin or ciprofloxacin.

Bacteria with a thin peptidoglycan layer and an outer membrane containing lipopolysaccharide (endotoxin), which stain pink on Gram stain. Outer membrane makes them harder to treat with some antibiotics.
Velocity-dependent increase in muscle tone with hyperreflexia, from upper motor neuron lesions. Classic clasp-knife spasticity gives resistance that suddenly gives way.
The two components of a ribosome. Prokaryotes have 30S and 50S subunits (70S total) and eukaryotes have 40S and 60S (80S), which are targets of different antibiotics.
Glial cells that myelinate peripheral nerve axons, one segment of one axon each, and aid nerve regeneration. Destroyed in Guillain-Barre syndrome; give rise to schwannomas.
A family of liver enzymes that metabolize most drugs and steroids. Inducers (rifampin, phenytoin, carbamazepine) lower drug levels; inhibitors (ketoconazole, cimetidine, grapefruit juice) raise them.
Hydrochloric acid secreted by parietal cells of the stomach, stimulated by gastrin, histamine and acetylcholine. Blocked by proton pump inhibitors and H2 blockers.
A low neutrophil count (below about 1500 per microliter), raising risk of serious bacterial and fungal infection. Causes include chemotherapy, drugs and congenital disorders.
Infection of the liver by hepatitis C virus, an RNA flavivirus spread by blood. Often becomes chronic, leading to cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma; cured by direct-acting antivirals.
A T cell growth factor made by activated helper T cells that stimulates proliferation of T cells and NK cells. Targeted by calcineurin inhibitors, which block its production.
An anticonvulsant that blocks sodium channels, used for partial seizures, trigeminal neuralgia and bipolar disorder. Causes SIADH, agranulocytosis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome and induces CYP450.
A sugar found in fruit and honey, metabolized in the liver by fructokinase and aldolase B. Aldolase B deficiency causes hereditary fructose intolerance with hypoglycemia and liver injury.
Coughing up blood from the lower respiratory tract. Causes include bronchiectasis, tuberculosis, lung cancer and pulmonary embolism.
Breast cancer arising from the milk duct epithelium. Invasive ductal carcinoma is the most common breast cancer; DCIS is confined within the ducts.
Mood disorder with persistent low mood or loss of interest plus sleep, appetite and energy changes. Treated with SSRIs, psychotherapy and in severe cases ECT.
Vitamin B3, a precursor of NAD and NADP. Deficiency causes pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia); high doses lower LDL and raise HDL but cause flushing.
Inflammation of the kidney's interstitium and tubules, often a drug hypersensitivity to NSAIDs, penicillins or diuretics. Presents with fever, rash, eosinophilia and white blood cell casts.
A single-stranded DNA virus infecting red cell precursors. Causes fifth disease (slapped-cheek rash), aplastic crisis in sickle cell disease and hydrops fetalis in pregnancy.
Cerebral lobe involved in hearing, language comprehension (Wernicke area), memory (hippocampus) and emotion (amygdala). Lesions can cause receptive aphasia and Kluver-Bucy syndrome.
Enveloped, positive-sense single-stranded RNA viruses with spike proteins. Cause common colds as well as SARS, MERS and COVID-19.
Benign enlargement of male breast tissue from an elevated estrogen-to-androgen ratio. Causes include puberty, cirrhosis, and drugs such as spironolactone and ketoconazole.
Narrowing of the mitral valve, most often from rheumatic heart disease. Causes an opening snap and diastolic rumble, with left atrial enlargement and risk of atrial fibrillation.
A cervical cytology screening test that detects precancerous squamous changes caused by HPV. Findings are classified from ASC-US to high-grade lesions.
Inflammation of the esophagus. Causes include reflux, Candida and herpes in immunocompromised patients, pill injury, and eosinophilic disease.
Proteins that bind specific DNA sequences to turn gene transcription on or off. Examples are p53, NF-kB and steroid hormone receptors.
Adrenal enzyme needed to make cortisol and aldosterone. Deficiency is the most common cause of congenital adrenal hyperplasia, causing virilization, salt wasting and high 17-hydroxyprogesterone.
Reduced secretion of one or more pituitary hormones, causing secondary adrenal, thyroid and gonadal failure. Causes include tumors, Sheehan syndrome and pituitary apoplexy.
Proteins on lipoprotein surfaces that structure the particle and direct metabolism, such as ApoB-100, ApoB-48, ApoA-I, ApoC-II and ApoE.
Inflammation of the bronchi causing cough. Acute bronchitis is usually viral; chronic bronchitis is defined as productive cough for 3 months in 2 years and is part of COPD.
Low blood pH from CO2 retention due to hypoventilation. Occurs in COPD, opioid overdose and neuromuscular weakness.
Primary liver cancer arising in hepatocytes, usually in cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis B or C. Marked by raised alpha-fetoprotein and spread into the portal vein.
The enzyme at synapses that breaks down acetylcholine into acetate and choline, ending the signal. Blocked by organophosphates and drugs like neostigmine.

A chronic autoimmune skin disease with well-demarcated silvery-scaled plaques on extensor surfaces, from keratinocyte hyperproliferation. Features include Auspitz sign, nail pitting and association with arthritis.
A basal ganglia nucleus that outputs inhibitory signals to the thalamus. Affected in Parkinson disease circuits, and damaged by carbon monoxide poisoning.
The delicate middle layer of the meninges, below the dura. Subarachnoid space beneath it holds cerebrospinal fluid; bleeding into it causes subarachnoid hemorrhage.
CNS glial cells that myelinate multiple axons, each cell wrapping many segments. Targeted in multiple sclerosis and progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy.
Premature separation of the placenta from the uterine wall, causing painful vaginal bleeding and a tense uterus. Risks are hypertension, cocaine and trauma; can cause fetal distress and DIC.

Fetal growth below the 10th percentile for gestational age, from placental insufficiency, maternal disease or infection. Symmetric forms usually start early; asymmetric forms are from late placental problems.
The CSF-filled cavity between the pons/medulla and cerebellum, draining via the foramina of Luschka and Magendie. Blockage or tumors here, such as medulloblastoma, cause hydrocephalus.
The selective barrier formed by tight junctions of brain capillary endothelium, astrocyte foot processes and basement membrane. It blocks many drugs and large polar molecules from entering the CNS.

Acute complication of insulin deficiency, mainly type 1 diabetes, with hyperglycemia, ketone production and metabolic acidosis. Features are Kussmaul breathing, fruity breath and dehydration; treated with fluids and insulin.
Swelling of the kidney from backed-up urine due to urinary tract obstruction, such as stones, prostatic enlargement or tumors. Prolonged obstruction damages kidney tissue.
Female sex chromosome disorder, usually 45,XO. Features are short stature, webbed neck, streak ovaries with primary amenorrhea, shield chest, coarctation of the aorta and horseshoe kidney.
The serous membrane lining the abdominal cavity (parietal) and covering organs (visceral). Parietal peritoneum is pain-sensitive; infection causes peritonitis.
Inflammatory bowel disease limited to the colon and rectum, with continuous mucosal inflammation causing bloody diarrhea. Linked to primary sclerosing cholangitis, p-ANCA and colorectal cancer risk.
